text:
**Marginalia**

The first correction appeared in October, in a copy of *The Old Man and the Sea* that had circulated through the Kettle Harbor library forty-one times. Marion Reyes found it while shelving: a faint pencil mark under the word *gulf*, and in the margin, in a small, upright hand, *Gulf Stream—capital S. He'd have wanted it.*

She should have erased it. Pencil in library books was a small vandalism, and she kept a gum eraser in the desk drawer for exactly this purpose. Instead she stood in the stacks with the book open, gulls arguing on the roof of the hardware store next door, and felt something she couldn't quite name. It wasn't annoyance. It was closer to the feeling of overhearing a conversation meant for someone else—someone more attentive than she was.

The next week, a biography of Rachel Carson came back with a date circled in the text. *Wrong year,* the margin said. *She left the Bureau in 1952, not 1951. Check the letters.* Marion checked. The corrector was right.

She began to watch the returns. Kettle Harbor was a town of eleven thousand people, a working harbor that had half-turned tourist, with a library housed in a converted cannery office—wood floors, salt-fogged windows, a children's room where the ceiling pipes clanked in winter. The library had 2,300 cardholders and a returns bin that Marion emptied herself most afternoons. She started keeping a list of the corrected books, and the list had a shape to it. Nonfiction, mostly. History. Nature. The occasional novel, but only if the novel had gotten a fact wrong.

In November, a field guide to Pacific shorebirds came back with a note beside the illustration of a marbled godwit: *This is a bar-tailed. The drawing is fine; the label is wrong. Whoever wrote this caption never held either bird.*

Marion sat down at the circulation desk and looked at the list. She knew the handwriting now, the way you know a neighbor's walk. She had a suspicion, and the suspicion had a name.

Walter Gee had been coming to the library on Tuesdays and Fridays for as long as Marion had worked there—first as a page, then as the librarian, eleven years in total. He was eighty-two, a former commercial fisherman who had also, improbably, spent two winters in the sixties working as a proofreader for a printing outfit in Eureka, a fact she'd learned from his late wife, Ruth, who had volunteered at the front desk until her death four years ago. Walter took out four books at a time and returned them exactly on time, and he never spoke more than a few words. *Good book. Slow going. Thanks, Marion.*

The following Tuesday, she checked his returns. Three books, clean. The fourth was a history of the Pacific salmon fishery, and there, on page 212, in the upright hand: *The canneries at Kettle Harbor closed in 1974, not 1971. I unloaded the last tender myself. October 3. It was raining.*

Marion held the book and looked across the reading room at Walter, who was doing the crossword with a pencil he had brought from home. He was a wide man gone narrow, with hands that had kept their size while the rest of him shrank, and he wore a wool cap indoors and out. She almost went over. She didn't. It felt like a door she shouldn't open by force.

Instead, she did something she'd never done in eleven years. She left him a note.

She wrote it in pencil on the margin of the salmon book's page 212, just below his correction: *Noted for the next edition. Do you remember the name of the tender?*

She shelved the book in the new-returns section and waited. Friday, Walter came in, took his books, and left without a word. But when she checked the salmon book, there was a reply: *The *Delia M*. She's a dive charter out of Monterey now. They painted her white. A shame.*

And so it began. For three weeks they exchanged notes in the margins of returned books, a slow correspondence conducted in pencil, about the salmon fishery, about the godwit and the bar-tailed godwit, about whether Hemingway would have wanted the capital S. Marion found herself choosing books for him deliberately—ones with errors she suspected he'd catch, ones with questions she wanted answered. He began to leave notes in books she hadn't asked about, and she understood that the game had widened, that he was reading her list now, reading her.

In December, on a Tuesday of hard rain, she brought the salmon book to his table instead of shelving it.

"Page 212," she said.

Walter looked up. His face did something complicated—not a smile, exactly, but a loosening. "You didn't erase it."

"I should have. It's policy."

"Policy," he said, as if tasting the word. "Ruth had a policy about people writing in books. She'd have skinned me."

"She probably knew."

"She knew everything." He turned the book over in his big hands. "I started doing it after she passed. Couldn't sleep. Reading was the only thing that worked, and I got in the habit of—talking back to the books. Arguing with them. Then I couldn't stop. I kept the pencil. I'm sorry about that. I'll pay for the damage."

"There's no damage. I can erase it. I've been erasing some." She sat down across from him. "The ones I could verify, I sent to the publishers. Two of them. The godwit and the Carson date. The Carson one—they wrote back. They're fixing it in the next printing."

Walter was quiet for a long moment. The rain came hard against the windows, and somewhere in the children's room the pipes clanked. "Ruth used to say I had a head full of cargo and nowhere to unload it," he said. "Fifty years of fish and weather and boat names, and everybody who'd have cared about it is gone."

"I care about it," Marion said. "I've been writing to you in the margins for three weeks. I hope you noticed."

"I noticed." He looked at her then, really looked, the way she imagined he'd once looked at weather coming in. "You write a good clear hand, Marion. You'd have made a decent proofreader."

"I'd have made a terrible proofreader. I don't know anything."

"You know how to check a date. That's most of it." He tapped the book. "The rest is just caring whether
